passage:
Tuesday: Ojas got stuck on the fraction word problem and threw his pencil down. Harish sir came over. "What have you tried?" "Nothing works." "Try drawing it," Harish sir said, and moved on.
Wednesday: Ojas tried drawing pizzas. Wrong. Then counting in steps. Wrong. Then a number line, and it worked. Harish sir crouched by his desk. "You tried three different ways, and when the first two didn't work, you switched. That's exactly how people get good at maths."
Friday: When Harish sir offered a harder bonus sheet, Ojas's hand shot up first. "Can I try the number line on these?" He got four out of six, and he was grinning.

qa.q: What method finally worked for Ojas on Wednesday?
qa.a: A number line.

qa.q: Why was Ojas's hand the first to shoot up on Friday?
qa.a: Harish sir's praise showed him that switching methods is how people get good, so he felt confident and eager, seeing a harder sheet as a chance rather than a risk.

qa.q: What made Harish sir's praise work well?
qa.a: It named exactly what Ojas did, trying three ways and switching, rather than calling him clever, so he knew what to repeat.

qa.q: What would change if Harish sir had only said "Good boy, you're clever"?
qa.a: Ojas might not know what helped, and could even avoid the bonus sheet in case it made him look less clever.

grounding: A teacher praises a child's strategy switching, and the child begins seeking harder problems.

passage: Imran, you asked how to encourage the weaker ones in your class. Let me tell you about a girl called Pinki, from my first year teaching in Nagpur, when the children called me Usha teacher. She was nine and she hated long division. One day I watched her try it the book way and fail, then try splitting the number into hundreds and tens and fail, then try guessing and checking, and get it right. Before, I'd have said "good girl, clever girl". That day I said, "Pinki, you tried three ways and didn't give up. That's how you got it." She looked at me as if no one had ever said that to her. The next week she asked for the hard sums. Praise what they did, beta, not what they are.

qa.q: What three ways did Pinki try for long division?
qa.a: The book way, splitting the number into hundreds and tens, and guessing and checking.

qa.q: Why did Pinki look at Usha teacher as if no one had ever said that?
qa.a: She was surprised and moved to be praised for her persistence rather than her cleverness; it showed her that her effort mattered.

qa.q: What choice does Usha urge Imran to make in class?
qa.a: To praise what the children do, their methods and persistence, rather than what they are, so they reach for harder work.

qa.q: How might Imran use this story with the weaker students?
qa.a: Imran might watch for a child trying different approaches and name it aloud, helping that child see progress as something they can build.

grounding: An elder teacher recalls praising a child's methods and persistence, after which the child sought harder problems.

passage: The Class 6 room at the government school had fifty-two students and one fan, and Francis sir had only ten minutes before the bell. Samir was still bent over the geometry problem most had skipped, having tried measuring with a broken ruler, then folding the paper, then drawing a grid on the back. Francis sir, squeezing between benches with forty notebooks still to check, stopped anyway. "Samir, show me." Samir showed the grid. "You tried folding, and when that didn't work you made a grid. That was smart work, not luck." The bell rang. Samir packed slowly, still looking at the grid. The next day, Samir came to the staffroom door with another problem from the back of the book. "Sir, I want to try this one."

qa.q: What did Samir draw on the back of the paper?
qa.a: A grid.

qa.q: Why did Samir pack slowly, still looking at the grid?
qa.a: Samir seemed proud and thoughtful, taking in that the grid was good work, not luck, and that switching methods had paid off.

qa.q: Which choice by Francis sir mattered most under the time pressure?
qa.a: Stopping for a moment despite the crowded room and the notebooks, and naming Samir's exact strategy rather than just saying "well done".

qa.q: What would change if Francis sir had walked past without stopping?
qa.a: Samir might have left without knowing the grid idea was valuable, and might not have come to the staffroom asking for a harder problem.

grounding: Despite a crowded class and little time, a teacher praises a child's switch of strategy, and the child seeks more challenge.

passage: In the Class 3 room of a Hyderabad school, Aparna had been stuck on the same puzzle for ten minutes: move matchsticks to make three triangles out of nine sticks. First she laid them in a row. Then she tried a star. Then she drew it on paper, rubbed it out, and tried again, tongue between her teeth. Finally the three triangles clicked. Rukmini Ma'am came over. "Aparna, I watched you. You tried a row, then a star, then you drew it out. When one way didn't work, you changed the way. That's why you got it." Aparna looked at her matchsticks, then up. "Can I try the harder one? The four triangles?" Rukmini Ma'am smiled and handed her the card.

qa.q: How many matchsticks did Aparna have to work with?
qa.a: Nine sticks.

qa.q: Why does Aparna ask for the harder puzzle right away?
qa.a: Hearing that changing her approach is what worked made her feel she could do it again, so a harder puzzle seemed exciting rather than risky.

qa.q: Which part of Rukmini Ma'am's praise mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Naming the exact steps, row, star, drawing, and the switch between them; it tells Aparna that her methods and persistence, not luck, solved the puzzle.

qa.q: How might a classmate who gave up early feel hearing Rukmini Ma'am's words?
qa.a: That classmate might realise that getting stuck is normal and that trying different ways is what worked, and feel encouraged to try again.

grounding: A teacher praises a child for changing methods until one worked, and the child immediately seeks a harder challenge.

passage:
"Mausi, I got it! The kite-string sum!"
Ishita Mausi put down her tea. "The one you called impossible at lunch?"
"Yes! First I tried adding, wrong. Then I drew the kite and the string, still wrong. Then I made a table like you do on your board."
"Show me." Mausi read the page slowly. "Aditi, look at what you did. You didn't stop when adding failed. You drew it. When the drawing didn't work, you changed again. The table worked because you'd already ruled out two ways."
"So I'm good at maths?"
"You're getting better at maths, because you kept changing your way in. That's how it grows. I see it in my Class 5 kids too."
Aditi flipped to a fresh page. "Then give me the tough one from your box."

qa.q: What three methods did Aditi try?
qa.a: Adding, drawing the kite and the string, and making a table.

qa.q: What does Aditi's 'So I'm good at maths?' suggest Aditi is thinking?
qa.a: Aditi feels proud and excited, and is checking whether success means a fixed talent; it hints at a pull toward labels, which Mausi gently turns toward effort.

qa.q: What choice does Ishita Mausi make in her answer, and why does it help?
qa.a: She describes each method and says ability grows by changing approaches; that makes Aditi want the tough problem instead of protecting a label.

qa.q: How might Ishita Mausi feel when Aditi asks for the tough one?
qa.a: Ishita Mausi is probably delighted 😊, seeing that praise for the process has made a challenge feel inviting rather than scary.

grounding: An aunt who is a teacher praises a child's switching of methods, teaching that ability grows, and the child asks for a harder problem.
